fieldFixes.contribution: Soltani was the primary technical consultant on The Wall Street Journal's 'What They Know' tracking investigation, Chief Technologist of the US Federal Trade Commission and an architect of California's CCPA and CPRA privacy laws, and his biographies credit him as a co-creator of Do Not Track. In October 2020 he and Sebastian Zimmeck launched Global Privacy Control with publishers, browsers and EFF, a browser setting that tells each site the user opts out of sale or sharing of their data, which California regulations require businesses to honour. On 4 October 2021 he became the first executive director of the California Privacy Protection Agency, serving until January 2025.

issues: The page numbers in the source notes are off by one. In the PDF (printed page numbers checked page by page with pdfminer), the 'informelle Gründung' sentence, the start of the TUWAT notice and '12.9.81' are on p. 58, not p. 57. The Kommune 1 table sentence and 'Zu dem Treffen sollen etwa 20 Personen gekommen sein' are on p. 61, not p. 60. The 'Wem gehören meine Daten?' topic line is on p. 59.

The title says the Chaos Computer Club 'is born' at this meeting, but the name did not exist yet. Röhr (printed p. 69, --check FOUND): 'Etwa gegen Ende des Jahres 1982 soll auch der Name „Chaos Computer Club“ für diesen Stammtisch in Verwendung gewesen sein.' The CCC itself calls the meeting its informal founding (ccc.de/de/club), so the title is reworded to say that and not imply the name existed in 1981.
'About 20 people came' is hedged in the source ('sollen ... gekommen sein', i.e. 'are said to have come'); the summary now says 'Some 20 people are said to have come'.

The other claims hold. The taz of 1 Sept 1981, p. 2 notice is headed 'TUWAT,TXT Version'. It is signed 'Tom Twiddlebit, Wau Wolf Ungenannt(»2)': Schleisiek, Holland, Gevert and two unnamed, i.e. Wulf Müller and Jochen Büttner, five Hamburg men linked through the Medienladen. The meeting was on 12.9.81 from 11.00 at 'Wattstr. (TAZ-Hauptgebäude)', and the topic list includes 'Datenrecht (Wem gehören meine Daten?)'. Coordinates 52.5414, 13.3897 match Wattstraße, 13355 Berlin (Gesundbrunnen, formerly Bezirk Wedding) per the Photon/OSM geocoder.

fieldFixes.title: 'Komputerfrieks' meet at the taz: the Chaos Computer Club's informal founding
fieldFixes.summary: A notice headed 'TUWAT,TXT Version' in the taz of 1 September 1981, signed by five Hamburg media activists including Wau Holland and Klaus Schleisiek, invited computer enthusiasts to meet at the paper's Wattstraße building on 12 September 1981. Some 20 people are said to have come, meeting at a large table that had once stood in the Kommune 1. The Chaos Computer Club counts this meeting as its informal founding, though the name itself seems to have come into use only around the end of 1982. The notice's topic list included data law under the question 'who owns my data?'.

issues: 'Bavarian officials later confirmed using the software in five cases' misstates the source. Help Net Security only relays a Süddeutsche Zeitung report that Bavarian agents used it in five cases. What officials confirmed (Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann, Monday 10 October 2011) was that the CCC's sample could be traced to a 2009 Bavarian police investigation (Tagesspiegel, Abendzeitung). The 'at least five cases' figure in the German press came from the Green MP Susanna Tausendfreund and the SZ. The summary is rewritten to separate the official confirmation from the reported count.

The significance field says the CCC 'showed that a person's computer had become part of the "core area of private life"'. That was the CCC's argument, not something it demonstrated; the release's own bracketed note says 'The CCC is basically arguing that nowadays a person's laptop is intrinsically part of this core area'. 'showed' is changed to 'argued'.

Source[0] note: the case number '1 BvR 370/07' is not on the CCC page. The release says only 'the German constitutional court ("Bundesverfassungsgericht") on February 27 2008'. The case number itself is correct, but it is not quoted from this source.

fieldFixes.summary: On 8 October 2011 the CCC published binaries and an analysis of 'lawful interception' malware used by German police, sent to it anonymously. It reported that software meant only to tap internet telephony could also take screenshots, load and run further programs and be taken over by third parties, because its commands were unencrypted and unauthenticated. The club argued this breached limits set by the Federal Constitutional Court in its 27 February 2008 ruling. Two days later Bavaria's interior ministry confirmed that the sample came from a 2009 Bavarian police investigation, and the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that Bavarian police had used the trojan in five cases.
fieldFixes.significance: Hackers, not a regulator, audited the state's own surveillance code, and argued that a person's computer had become part of the 'core area of private life'.
